chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Ma'bad, from Abdullah al-Dihqan, from Durust ibn Abu Mansur, from Atiyya, the brother of Abu al-Uram, who said:

I mentioned to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) the one who is copulated with from the men, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah will not afflict anyone with this affliction and there is a need for him. Indeed, in their behinds are inverted wombs, and the modesty of their behinds is like the modesty of the woman. A son of Iblis called Zawal has participated among them. So whoever among the men he has participated in is the passive one, and whoever among the women he participates in are the ones from whom the men act upon this. And the one acting upon this among the men, when he reaches forty years, does not leave it. And they are the remnant of Sodom. Indeed, I do not mean by their remnant that they are their children, but they are from their essence.'

He said: I said, 'Sodom which was turned upside down?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is four cities: Sodom, and Sareem, and Ladma', and Umeyra'. He said: So Jibraeel (peace be upon him) came to them and they were uprooted to the boundaries of the seventh earth. So he placed his wing under the lowest of them and raised them all until the inhabitants of the sky of the world heard the barking of their dogs, then he turned them upside down.'

key_terms.الْمَنْكُوحَ: The passive partner in homosexual intercourse
key_terms.زَوَالٌ: A son of Iblis associated with this affliction

ai.seo_question: What is the theological and physical explanation for male homosexuality in Shia hadith literature?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who contextualizes male homosexuality not merely as a physical act but as a distinct spiritual affliction linked to the essence of Sodom, noting that the rectum possesses an 'inverted womb' and modesty akin to women. The Imam identifies a specific entity, Zawal, son of Iblis, associated with those who persist in this practice, distinguishing the 'remnant of Sodom' as sharing their spiritual nature rather than being their biological descendants. This highlights the Shia scholarly view of the condition as a unique category of sin with specific metaphysical origins.
